Unquestionably, what makes Saul Goodman such a great character is his million-dollar mouthpiece. His smooth rhetoric and earnest, yet oleaginous charisma. The way he talks conveys a spirit of resourcefulness and optimism with a kind of unselfconscious garishness that is an emblem of the greatness of the American spirit.

However, I feel that the potential of this character is being left unfulfilled by a shortage of clever dialogue in the first two episodes.

His negotiation with Tuco in episode 2 was hackneyed, and frankly disappointing. It was nothing more than haggling, and frankly, any old woman at a flea market would have done better. The scene at the bar with the breadsticks featured no dialogue. Does anyone want to hear how he talks to a women in a bar? Well, I sure do! Why keep us hanging? It's a wasted opportunity to add dimension to his character and for maybe a little comedy. Music and slo-mo? Please! Inappropriate. The courtroom montage just had a bunch of single isolated phrases, and not very many of them, to boot.

Tuco thinks Saul "has a mouth on him"? Well, show us!

The whole series will be about him turning into that Saul.

It's going to be a great journey with ups and downs, and hopefully a lot of explanations on how money laundering works, using plenty of to-hand objects as visual aids. (No matter how correct that is, it's just hard to write visual aids somehow)

Saul does show a glimpse of this prowess with Tuco, but he's not there yet, he's browbeaten, down, going through hell.

Wait for it.

Exactly. He's not even called Saul yet, he's Jimmy McGill. It's like Walter White before he was Heisenberg. (although perhaps in the first few episodes of Breaking Bad you could already notice Walters assertiveness).

You can already see where Saul is going. His career is not going as he had hoped, and he's finding out money can be made other ways. At this point it looks like Nacho Varga is going to be his gateway into the underworld. I'm wondering what the story behind Mike is, though.

I do appreciate that, however, awesome as the first two episodes were, I did feel that they cheaped out on dialogue slightly. The scenes above were missed opportunities, they went with a faux "high-concept" thing in the montage and bar scene.

I'm probably applying too high a standard, as this is just a TV show, but my expectations were very high.

I think everyone had the same expectation, but I think it's been made abundantly clear that he's not that guy yet - we're all waiting for him to become that guy - it's a nod / recycle of the transformations in breaking bad.

I think Odenkirk is going to absolutely nail the transformations from reticent bending the rules lawyer to smooth talking ambulance chaser with shady customers.

I expected a big blow-up/crisis of conscience like happened with Chuck in the previous episode. Still, BCS is one of the best shows on television.
